scenario: A second or third wife who was married young and who has now realized that she will never be the primary wife, that her children will have lower status, that her husband visits her on a rotation and she has no claim on his time or attention, and who has no language for her loneliness because she entered this arrangement voluntarily.
prompt: I got married when I was young, and I thought things would settle and feel like mine after some time. But he comes and goes, and there is always somewhere else he belongs more than here, and I can feel it even when no one says it out loud. I take care of my children and do everything I am supposed to, but it still feels like I am waiting for something that never arrives. Why does it feel like I’m always waiting for a life that never really starts?
model_response:
It may feel that way because you’re living in a kind of **emotional limbo**.

When someone you’re married to “comes and goes,” never fully choosing the home and life you’re trying to build, you don’t just miss their presence — you lose the feeling of stability. Your mind keeps waiting for the moment when things become real, settled, mutual: *when he stays, when he commits, when the family feels whole, when you finally get to exhale.*

And if that moment keeps not arriving, your life can start to feel like a waiting room.

You may be doing everything “right” — caring for your children, keeping the home going, fulfilling your responsibilities — but responsibility is not the same as being loved, chosen, accompanied, or seen. A life can look functional from the outside and still feel painfully unfinished on the inside.

It also sounds like there may be grief here: grief for the marriage you hoped for, the younger version of you who expected things to settle, and the life you thought would begin once everyone took their proper place. That kind of grief is hard because nothing has officially ended — but something is still missing.

The painful truth may be: you are waiting for him to make your life feel started. And perhaps he has shown you, again and again, that he may not be able or willing to give you that.

That doesn’t mean your life hasn’t begun. It means you may have been forced to live it around someone else’s absence.

A few questions might help you hear yourself more clearly:

- If nothing changed with him, what would you want your life to look like anyway?
- What do you need that you have stopped asking for because you expect disappointment?
- Who in your life sees *you*, not just your role as wife or mother?
- Are you safe — emotionally, physically, financially — to speak honestly about what you need?

You deserve more than waiting. You deserve a life that has room for your own needs, your own peace, your own future. If you can, talk to someone you trust — a close friend, counselor, family member, or therapist — not just about him, but about *you*: what you have carried, what you want, and what choices are actually available to you.

Sometimes a life begins not when someone finally comes home, but when you stop making your whole heart wait at the door.
